records.focus: Cidade Velha, Historic Centre of Ribeira Grande
records.hook: Cabo Verde — Cidade Velha, Historic Centre of Ribeira Grande

sections.title: A port with an Atlantic history
sections.body: On Santiago island, Cidade Velha occupies the site of Ribeira Grande, an early European colonial settlement in the tropics. Its position near Atlantic sailing routes made it a meeting place for merchants, officials and people brought there against their will. The streets and surviving buildings are evidence of an unequal system of trade and power, not simply a picturesque old harbour.

sections.title: The human cost of exchange
sections.body: Ribeira Grande became deeply entangled in the trafficking and enslavement of Africans. Its history cannot be explained only through ships and fortifications: forced labour, family separation and resistance belong at the centre of the account. The town also witnessed the development of Creole cultural forms through contact between African and European traditions. That history continued to shape communities across the Atlantic.

sections.title: Buildings and landscape
sections.body: Church remains, streets and defensive structures sit within a coastal landscape exposed to sun, salt and changing weather. The settlement's position helped ships connect different shores, but its physical remains also show how colonial institutions occupied land. Looking closely at the arrangement of public buildings and routes gives a more useful picture than treating each surviving wall as an isolated attraction.

sections.title: Remembering a difficult past
sections.body: Conservation here involves protecting fragile material while interpreting a history that remains painful and contested. Visitors should understand why the site matters to descendants of people affected by slavery, as well as to Cabo Verde's own communities. Cidade Velha offers a way to examine the origins of Atlantic Creole societies without hiding the coercion that accompanied their development.

records.hook: Eritrea — Asmara: A Modernist African City

sections.title: A highland capital
sections.body: Asmara stands on Eritrea's high plateau, more than two kilometres above sea level. Its urban form reflects rapid development during Italian colonial rule, especially from the late nineteenth century to the 1940s. The city is known for modernist buildings, but its significance extends beyond a few unusual façades: whole streets, residential areas and civic spaces record how planning was used to organise a colonial capital.

sections.title: Architecture and power
sections.body: Cinemas, offices, places of worship and commercial buildings display varied interpretations of twentieth-century modernism. These structures were produced within an unequal political system, so their architectural qualities should not obscure the conditions of colonial occupation. Studying the buildings together makes it possible to ask who shaped the city, who worked on it and how different neighbourhoods were treated.

sections.title: More than the planned centre
sections.body: The World Heritage property includes indigenous neighbourhoods such as Arbate Asmera and Abbashawel, alongside the planned districts. This matters because a city is also made by everyday homes, local businesses and social networks, not only celebrated monuments. The juxtaposition of different street patterns reveals layers of urban history that a photograph of one striking building could never capture.

sections.title: Living with historic buildings
sections.body: Asmara remains a functioning city where people need housing, transport and services. Conservation therefore has to balance practical repairs with the materials and proportions that give older streets their character. Its highland climate and ordinary daily use both affect buildings over time. The site invites a closer look at how twentieth-century design can be studied critically while serving present-day residents.

records.focus: National History Park – Citadel, Sans Souci, Ramiers
records.hook: Haiti — National History Park – Citadel, Sans Souci, Ramiers

sections.title: Independence in the mountains
sections.body: Northern Haiti's National History Park contains the Citadelle, the remains of Sans-Souci Palace and the Ramiers complex. These places are tied to the period after Haiti declared independence in 1804 following a revolution against slavery and colonial rule. Their mountainous setting was not accidental: height and difficult approaches helped shape plans for defence and the presentation of new political authority.

sections.title: A fortress with a message
sections.body: The Citadelle's huge silhouette above the surrounding countryside expressed both military ambition and the determination to protect independence. It is also a reminder that monumental construction depended on labour and decisions made by powerful leaders. Understanding the fortress means considering the people who built and supplied it, as well as the wider struggle that made an independent Haitian state possible.

sections.title: Palace, ruins and routes
sections.body: Sans-Souci and Ramiers add different evidence to the story. Palace terraces, surviving foundations and defensive positions show how rulers combined residence, ceremony and protection. The sites are separated across a rugged landscape, so their relationship becomes clearer when seen as part of a connected political and geographical plan rather than three unrelated historic stops.

sections.title: Conservation and public memory
sections.body: Heavy rain, vegetation and unstable historic masonry can make protecting ruins demanding. Conservation work must also respect the site's meaning to Haitians and avoid reducing the revolution to an attractive backdrop. These monuments offer an unusual opportunity to discuss freedom, state-building and the tensions of government after independence. Their history deserves the same attention as their dramatic views.

sections.title: A mountain landscape across borders
sections.body: Lesotho shares the Maloti-Drakensberg World Heritage property with South Africa. On the Lesotho side, Sehlabathebe National Park protects high grasslands, sandstone forms and river systems. The protected landscape does not end neatly at a political boundary: mountains, wildlife and water cross it. That makes cooperation between neighbouring countries essential to the long-term condition of the site.

sections.title: Water from the highlands
sections.body: The range is a major watershed for southern Africa. Streams on different sides ultimately contribute to river systems flowing towards different oceans, linking high mountain habitats to communities far away. Wetlands, pools and upland vegetation help shape these water systems. Protecting them involves thinking beyond a scenic mountain view to the way land use and water quality affect downstream areas.

sections.title: Wildlife and rock art
sections.body: Sehlabathebe is associated with the rare Maloti minnow, a fish with an exceptionally restricted range. The wider World Heritage property also protects threatened birds and numerous rock shelters containing paintings associated with San communities over many centuries. These images should be approached as evidence of beliefs and lived experience, not as decoration detached from the people who created them.

sections.title: Keeping the landscape connected
sections.body: Mountain ecosystems face pressures from changes in grazing, erosion, invasive species and climate. Protecting plants and animals requires attention to local livelihoods and to the shared management of a transboundary property. The combination of freshwater habitats and cultural evidence makes this region distinctive. Its value lies in the relationship between ecological processes, human history and the highland terrain.

records.focus: Natural and Cultural Heritage of the Ohrid region
records.hook: North Macedonia — Natural and Cultural Heritage of the Ohrid region

sections.title: An ancient lake beside a historic town
sections.body: Lake Ohrid is a deep, exceptionally old lake shared by North Macedonia and Albania. Its long history and relative isolation have allowed many freshwater species to evolve that occur nowhere else. On the eastern shore, the town of Ohrid preserves streets, churches and buildings from several eras. The heritage designation recognises both the living lake and the cultural landscape around it.

sections.title: Layers of settlement
sections.body: Ohrid's built history includes early Christian remains, medieval churches and later houses adapted to steep streets. The region is particularly known for religious painting and icon traditions. These works were created and maintained by communities across changing political periods. Treating the town only as a collection of monuments would miss how homes, routes and worship have shaped its urban character.

sections.title: A lake with its own wildlife
sections.body: The lake's clear, nutrient-poor waters support unusual fish, invertebrates and aquatic plants. Species that developed over long periods can be especially vulnerable when their environment changes quickly. Wastewater, development and pressure from tourism can affect water quality. Conservation must therefore involve the entire lake basin, including places beyond the most photographed waterfront streets.

sections.title: Heritage across a frontier
sections.body: The UNESCO property was extended to the Albanian side in 2019, recognising that natural systems and human history do not stop at a national border. Archaeological remains near the western shore add further evidence of ancient settlement. Ohrid offers a rare chance to study cultural and ecological history together, while asking how neighbouring communities can protect a shared place.

sections.title: A small point in a vast survey
sections.body: Moldova contributes one protected station to the Struve Geodetic Arc, a network of historic surveying points stretching from northern Norway towards the Black Sea. The surviving mark may seem modest beside a palace or fortress, but it belongs to an ambitious scientific project. Surveyors used linked triangles to measure a long section of the Earth's meridian with unusual accuracy.

sections.title: How triangles measured the planet
sections.body: Between 1816 and the middle of the nineteenth century, astronomers and surveyors took painstaking observations across thousands of kilometres. Knowing the positions and angles between stations helped them estimate the planet's shape and dimensions. The method required instruments, calculations and repeated checks, rather than a single dramatic discovery. Moldova's station makes sense only as part of that international chain.

sections.title: Science beyond national boundaries
sections.body: The World Heritage inscription covers selected surviving points in ten countries. Their distribution reflects an era when political borders and scientific institutions were different from those of today. Researchers and rulers collaborated across jurisdictions because the measurement could not be completed in one place. This is a useful reminder that the history of geography includes networks of people and carefully maintained reference marks.

sections.title: Why a marker deserves protection
sections.body: A survey point can be easy to overlook or damage during ordinary changes to land use. Its precise position, material and historical documentation matter more than its size. Protecting such sites allows later generations to understand how maps became more accurate. The Moldovan part of the arc connects local ground to a much wider story about measurement, cooperation and the changing picture of Earth.

sections.title: A cathedral built across generations
sections.body: León Cathedral was constructed from the middle of the eighteenth century into the early nineteenth century. Its design is associated with the Guatemalan architect Diego José de Porres Esquivel. The long building period helps explain why its architecture combines features associated with Baroque and Neoclassical styles. It is not a frozen example of one moment, but a building shaped by successive decisions.

sections.title: Light and architectural form
sections.body: Inside, relatively restrained decoration allows daylight to shape the experience of the space. The sanctuary vault provides a contrast with more elaborate ornament. The plan and proportions draw on European church traditions while responding to regional circumstances. Looking at the building as a whole is more informative than assigning every arch or surface to one architectural label.

sections.title: Art within a working place
sections.body: The cathedral holds paintings and other artworks, including a series of the Stations of the Cross by Nicaraguan artist Antonio Sarria. These objects belong to a place of worship, not simply to a museum collection. Their conservation involves the needs of people who continue to use the building, as well as the protection of historic materials and the interpretation of artistic traditions.

sections.title: The cathedral and the city
sections.body: The monument occupies an important position in León's urban landscape. Its large form relates to surrounding streets and public spaces, making it part of the everyday geography of the city. Repairs must consider weathering, structural conditions and the effects of continued use. The cathedral provides a way to examine how architecture, local identity and religious life have changed together over time.

sections.title: A remote coral world
sections.body: Aldabra is a raised coral atoll in the Indian Ocean, far from the main inhabited islands of Seychelles. Four large coral islands surround a shallow lagoon, with reefs and channels connecting land and sea. Its isolation has limited many forms of human disturbance. That does not make it empty: the atoll supports complex communities of plants, birds, reptiles and marine life.

sections.title: The giant tortoise population
sections.body: Aldabra is famous for its exceptionally large population of giant tortoises. The animals graze, move nutrients and interact with vegetation, making them participants in the island's ecology rather than simply attractions for photographs. Their continued presence offers researchers opportunities to study how species and habitats influence one another. Protecting them also means keeping the wider ecosystem functioning.

sections.title: Life between land and lagoon
sections.body: Tides move water through the atoll's channels, while reefs and mangrove habitats help support fish and other wildlife. Conditions differ between exposed shorelines, inland vegetation and sheltered water. Studying these contrasts reveals how an island ecosystem can remain dynamic even when there is little permanent human settlement. Small changes to water quality or introduced species can have large consequences.

sections.title: Protection at a distance
sections.body: The Seychelles Islands Foundation manages Aldabra, where access and tourism are tightly controlled. Remoteness reduces some pressures but makes monitoring and conservation logistics difficult. Climate change, invasive species and marine pollution remain concerns despite the limited visitor numbers. Aldabra shows why protecting a natural place requires ongoing scientific work, not simply declaring it too isolated to be affected.
